extracted.intended_audience: writers, critics, and literate readers interested in aesthetics and literary judgment
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for judging art, artists, satire, and national literatures — drawn from Chesterton's critical essay on Whistler and cultural myths about 'young' nations. Useful for critics and creative writers assessing artistic character and originality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permanent substance of morality
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a permanent substance of morality, as much as there is a permanent substance of art; to say that the morality of one age can be entirely different from another 'means literally nothing at all.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should look for enduring ethical qualities underlying different moral codes rather than dismissing all morality as historically relative. An 'ideal moralist would see the enduring ethic under every code' — evaluate continuity and shared moral substance across periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art-versus-morality claims must be embodied
rubrics_metrics.description: The modern aesthete who claims 'morality should be wholly subordinated to art' often only favors a particular kind of moral conduct; to prove interest in art alone he would have to live in ways inconsistent with his moral preferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an artist or critic advocates 'art for art's sake,' check whether their life and choices demonstrate genuine disinterestedness. Anti-pattern: praising l'art pour l'art while clinging to distinct moral or social tastes (reading Mallarme but drinking absinthe, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency between artistic doctrine and personal behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: No man ever preached the impersonality of art so well; no man ever preached the impersonality of art so personally. (Whistler preached impersonality while incessantly talking about his rights and wrongs.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether an artist's public philosophy of art matches their personal conduct. A contradiction (preaching impersonality but living personally) undermines the sincerity and reliability of their aesthetic claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value artistic courage and dedication above mere talent
rubrics_metrics.description: Whistler's outstanding virtues were 'courage and an abstract love of good work.' A man must be something of a moralist to preach, even if preaching unmorality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In judging artists, give weight to perseverance, honest standards in workmanship (e.g., destroying a work rather than leaving a careless touch), and moral courage more than mere facility or novelty of talent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artistic temperament as a sign of amateurism
rubrics_metrics.description: The artistic temperament is a disease that afflicts amateurs; it arises from men not having sufficient power of expression to get rid of the element of art in their being.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be suspicious of self-conscious 'artistic temperaments' — excessive talk about art, continual aesthetic affectation, and inability to 'get rid' of the artistic impulse suggest an amateurish or diseased condition rather than genuine greatness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Great artist can dismiss art
rubrics_metrics.description: There can be no stronger manifestation of a really great artist than the fact that he can dismiss the subject of art; that he can, upon due occasion, wish art at the bottom of the sea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A test of greatness: capacity to be ordinary and to set aside art when necessary. If an artist cannot cease speaking of art, that is evidence of self-absorption and lesser stature.

rubrics_metrics.name: True wit involves laughter, not tortured malice
rubrics_metrics.description: Whistler's wit is 'a torture to him' — he twists himself into arabesques of verbal felicity and is inspired by 'the complete seriousness of sincere malice.' There was no laughter in his nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between wit that springs from ease, humility, or generosity (which can laugh at self and others) and cleverness that is clenched, malicious, or performed at self-cost. Prefer wit that shows thoughtlessness and self-abandonment (genuine laughter) over wit that is primarily injurious or self-justifying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms of great satire (three types)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three distinct classes of great satirists: (1) Rabelais-type who enjoys himself and his enemies (voluble, violent but not malicious); (2) Swift-type who rages from bitter unhappiness; (3) Pope/Atticus-type who satirises with pity and respect, pointing out strengths before weaknesses — the highest form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating satire, aim for the third type (satire tempered by pity and respect). Avoid satire motivated by self-vindication or mere spite (ascribed to Whistler); prefer satire that recognises the enemy's humanity and balances critique with acknowledgement of strengths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greatness shown by ordinariness and plainness
rubrics_metrics.description: All very great teachers and leaders assume their point of view to be human and casual; great minds address motley crowds with plainness and camaraderie (examples: Christ and Shakespeare).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gauge greatness by the ability to be ordinary — to discharge extraordinary impulses into ordinary life. Plain, prosaic communication that reaches common people is a sign of real intellectual or artistic stature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geniality as 'strength to spare'
rubrics_metrics.description: Geniality is almost definable as strength to spare; Whistler had no geniality because he lived 'up to his emotional incomes' and had no strength to spare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In judging character, see whether an artist has surplus energy for kindness and generosity; lack of geniality (constant taut vanity) signals a weaker personality despite technical gifts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger of low, practical ideals (false 'practicality')
rubrics_metrics.description: The most intoxicating and dangerous ideals are the tame, low ideals that are easy to think you have attained (e.g., wishing merely to be a 'gentleman'); high ideals sober rather than delude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing motives or character, beware claims to 'practical' or 'attainable' ideals that mask delusion and social dislocation. Prefer high, demanding ideals that avoid self-deception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not conflate chronological newness with artistic freshness
rubrics_metrics.description: The metaphor of youth applied to nations (America, New Zealand, colonies) is deceptive — chronological youth does not imply vigour, novelty, or moral/intellectual freshness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate colonial or 'new' literature and culture on intrinsic artistic merits rather than on supposed novelty due to recent origin. Avoid romanticizing 'young nations' as inherently vigorous or original.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality springs from genuine cultural difference, not mere geography
rubrics_metrics.description: The one striking colonial exception (Olive Schreiner) was original precisely because she was not English; South Africa is 'the one English colony which is not English.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek originality in authentic cultural divergence or different sensibilities rather than in mere setting. Exceptions to derivative work tend to come from writers rooted in different cultural traditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess national 'greatness' by heroism in government, arms, and art
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three main shapes in which a nation can show itself glad and great—by the heroic in government, by the heroic in arms, and by the heroic in art; one should judge a nation by these eternal tests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging a nation's cultural vitality, look to its institutions' capacity for noble governance, moral courage in conflict, and authentic artistic achievement, rather than superficial markers like population, money, or bustle.
